::: {#exr-prac-binom-lik}
#### Binomial likelihood (adapted from @dobson4e, Chapter 3)

Let $Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \prob)$,
so that

$$
\p(Y = y \mid \prob) = \binom{n}{y} \prob^y (1-\prob)^{n-y},
\quad y \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}.
$$

Assume $0 < y < n$ so the MLE lies in the interior of $(0, 1)$.

**(a)** Write the log-likelihood $\llik(\prob; y)$ for a single observation $y$.

**(b)** Derive the score function $\score(\prob; y) \eqdef \deriv{\prob}\llik(\prob; y)$.

**(c)** Set the score equal to zero and solve for $\hprob_{ML}$.
Confirm that $\hprob_{ML} = y/n$.

**(d)** Compute the second derivative $\hess(\prob; y)$ and verify that it is negative,
confirming a maximum.
:::

:::{#sol-prac-binom-lik}

**(a)**

$$
\ba
\llik(\prob; y)
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y} \prob^y (1-\prob)^{n-y}}
&& \text{(log of the binomial PMF)}
\\
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y}} + \logf{\prob^y} + \logf{(1-\prob)^{n-y}}
&& \text{(log of a product)}
\\
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y}} + y\logf{\prob} + (n-y)\logf{1-\prob}
&& \text{(log of a power)}
\ea
$$

The first term does not depend on $\prob$,
so it drops out of every derivative with respect to $\prob$.

**(b)**

$$
\ba
\score(\prob; y)
&= \deriv{\prob}\sb{\logf{\binom{n}{y}} + y\logf{\prob} + (n-y)\logf{1-\prob}}
&& \text{(log-likelihood from (a))}
\\
&= \deriv{\prob}\logf{\binom{n}{y}} + \deriv{\prob}\sb{y\logf{\prob}} + \deriv{\prob}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\prob}}
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= 0 + \deriv{\prob}\sb{y\logf{\prob}} + \deriv{\prob}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\prob}}
&& \text{(derivative of a constant)}
\\
&= \deriv{\prob}\sb{y\logf{\prob}} + \deriv{\prob}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\prob}}
&& \text{(drop the zero term)}
\\
&= y\deriv{\prob}\logf{\prob} + (n-y)\deriv{\prob}\logf{1-\prob}
&& \text{(constant multiple rule)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\prob} + (n-y)\deriv{\prob}\logf{1-\prob}
&& \text{(derivative of $\log$)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\prob} + (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\prob}\deriv{\prob}(1-\prob)
&& \text{(chain rule)}
\ea
$$

The inner derivative is:

$$
\ba
\deriv{\prob}(1-\prob)
&= \deriv{\prob} 1 - \deriv{\prob} \prob
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= 0 - \deriv{\prob} \prob
&& \text{(derivative of a constant)}
\\
&= 0 - 1
&& \text{(derivative of $\prob$ with respect to itself)}
\\
&= -1
&& \text{(subtract)}
\ea
$$

Substituting the inner derivative back in:

$$
\ba
\score(\prob; y)
&= y\frac{1}{\prob} + (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\prob}(-1)
&& \text{(inner derivative is $-1$)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\prob} - (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\prob}
&& \text{(multiply by $-1$)}
\\
&= \frac{y}{\prob} - \frac{n-y}{1-\prob}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{y(1-\prob)}{\prob(1-\prob)} - \frac{(n-y)\prob}{\prob(1-\prob)}
&& \text{(write both terms over the common denominator)}
\\
&= \frac{y(1-\prob) - (n-y)\prob}{\prob(1-\prob)}
&& \text{(combine the fractions)}
\\
&= \frac{y - y\prob - n\prob + y\prob}{\prob(1-\prob)}
&& \text{(expand the numerator)}
\\
&= \frac{y - n\prob}{\prob(1-\prob)}
&& \text{(cancel $y\prob$)}
\ea
$$

**(c)**

Setting $\score(\prob; y) = 0$:

$$
\ba
0 &= \frac{y - n\prob}{\prob(1-\prob)}
&& \text{(score from (b))}
\\
0 &= y - n\prob
&& \text{(multiply both sides by $\prob(1-\prob)$)}
\\
y &= n\prob
&& \text{(add $n\prob$ to both sides)}
\\
\hprob_{ML} &= \frac{y}{n}
&& \text{(divide both sides by $n$)}
\ea
$$

**(d)**

$$
\ba
\hess(\prob; y)
&= \deriv{\prob}\sb{\frac{y}{\prob} - \frac{n-y}{1-\prob}}
&& \text{(score from (b))}
\\
&= \deriv{\prob}\sb{y\prob^{-1} - (n-y)(1-\prob)^{-1}}
&& \text{(write the fractions as negative powers)}
\\
&= \deriv{\prob}\sb{y\prob^{-1}} - \deriv{\prob}\sb{(n-y)(1-\prob)^{-1}}
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= y\deriv{\prob}\prob^{-1} - (n-y)\deriv{\prob}(1-\prob)^{-1}
&& \text{(constant multiple rule)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\prob^{-2}} - (n-y)\deriv{\prob}(1-\prob)^{-1}
&& \text{(power rule)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\prob^{-2}} - (n-y)\paren{-(1-\prob)^{-2}}\deriv{\prob}(1-\prob)
&& \text{(chain rule, outer function $u^{-1}$)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\prob^{-2}} - (n-y)\paren{-(1-\prob)^{-2}}(-1)
&& \text{(inner derivative from (b) is $-1$)}
\\
&= -y\prob^{-2} - (n-y)(1-\prob)^{-2}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= -\frac{y}{\prob^2} - \frac{n-y}{(1-\prob)^2}
&& \text{(write the negative powers as fractions)}
\ea
$$

Since $y \geq 0$, $n - y \geq 0$, and $y$ and $n - y$ are not both zero,
$\hess(\prob; y) < 0$ for every $\prob \in (0,1)$.
So $\llik$ is strictly concave,
and its critical point $\hprob_{ML} = y/n$ is its global maximum.

:::
